Expressing Regret and Uncertainty in The Past: Should Have
You use the modal phrase should have to express regret and uncertainty about the past.

You use should have + past participle to talk about something that that would have been a good idea, but you didn't do it (in other words, when you regret something).

For example:
I should have tried harder in school.

You use shouldn't have + past participle to talk about something that wasn't a good idea, but you did it anyway (in other words, you regret something).

For example:
You shouldn't have gone out last night - now you're too tired to work.

You can also use should have + past participle to talk about something that, if everything is normal and okay, you think has already happened. It's often used with 'by now'.

For example:
Joe should have finished the test by now.
Other cars behind you could have hit you.
You could have just followed them.
We couldn't have stopped because the other cars coming wouldn't see us.
The Past Continuous vs. The Simple Past
You use the Simple Past, not the Past Continuous, to talk about repeated actions in the past.

For example:
We went to Japan four times last year.

When you want to emphasize that repeated actions continued for a temporary period of time, you can use the Past Continuous.

For example:
When my grandmother was sick, we were visiting her every day.
My mother was doing her best to see the road while driving and maintaining a constant speed.
What were you doing while your mom was driving?
My brother, John wasn't talking, and I wasn't talking either.
As mom was driving the wind was starting to blow.
The snow was swirling around the car and it was becoming impossible to see.

images.text:
Amy: It's really coming down out here. It reminds of a time when my mom tried to drive home in a white out.
Vanessa: I'm sorry, dear. What is a white out?
Amy: In the winter, it's when the snow-covered countryside is indistinguishable from the road due to the wind whipping up the snow.
Vanessa: Got it.
Amy: So one night my mother was driving my brother and I home from his basketball game in another county. It had snowed a lot all week. We were driving on some small Kansas road.
Peter: Wait! You are from Kansas?
Amy Yeah, Lucas, Kansas.
Peter: Yea! Haw!
Amy: Anyway, As mom was driving the wind was starting to blow. The snow was swirling around the car and it was becoming impossible to see.

Peter: Did you pull over?
Vanessa: They couldn't have pulled over.
Amy: Right. It's too dangerous. We couldn't have stopped because the other cars coming wouldn't see us and they'd crash into the back of us.
Peter: So what did you do?
Amy: We kept driving. My mother was doing her best to see the road while driving and maintaining a constant speed.

Peter: What were you doing while your mom was driving?
Amy: Nothing. My brother, John wasn't talking, and I wasn't talking either. We were scared. Finally, up ahead, we saw a pair of tail lights through the white out. They shone like a demon's eyes, but these lights were our saviors.
Vanessa: Right, because you could have just followed them.
Amy: Exactly! So we followed the tail lights wherever they went. We had been driving for a while, when the truck in front of us suddenly stopped.
Vanessa: Oh, no! Other cars behind you could have hit you.
Amy: My mom slammed on the brakes. She was yelling, “you can't stop here. You are going to get us killed!”
Peter: What happened?
Amy: Mom started honking the horn loudly. Finally, a man got out of the truck and walked back to our car. My mom rolled down the window and screamed, “you can't stop here.” The man replied, “Sure, I can.” My mom exclaimed, “Why?” To which the man responded, “because I'm home.”
Vanessa: WOW!
Peter: Wait! That story couldn't have happened!
Amy: Yeaah … ha!
